title: Limit source files to a single top-level class
concept: While the Java compiler lets you define multiple top-level classes in a single source file (.java), doing so provides no benefits and carries enormous risks. Putting multiple top-level classes in a single file makes it possible to provide multiple, conflicting definitions for a class depending on the order in which source files are passed to the compiler. The behavior of your program can literally depend on the order in which files are compiled. The rule is simple: never put multiple top-level classes or interfaces in a single source file. If multiple classes must reside in one file, make them static member classes.

when_to_use_flashcard.front: Why should you never declare multiple top-level classes in a single .java source file?
when_to_use_flashcard.back: It creates the risk of duplicate class definitions across files where the compiled program's behavior depends arbitrarily on the command-line order in which files are passed to javac.

when_not_to_use_flashcard.front: What is the alternative if you want multiple related helper classes in the same file?
when_not_to_use_flashcard.back: Declare them as static member classes (static inner classes) inside the primary class, preferably marked private or package-private.

quiz.question: What is the primary danger of placing multiple top-level classes in a single source file?
options: The compiler may accept conflicting duplicate class definitions whose resolution depends on the order files are passed to javac
It causes the JVM to run in interpreted mode only
It prevents the file from containing methods
The garbage collector crashes

quiz.question: How many `public` top-level classes can exist in a single Java source file?
options: At most one, and the filename must match the name of the public class exactly
As many as you want
None
Two, if they are both abstract

quiz.question: If you have small helper classes tightly coupled to a single class, where should they live?
options: As private static member classes inside that single class
In a separate package called 'helpers'
In the default package
Inside an interface constant

quiz.question: What happens if you run `javac Main.java Dessert.java` versus `javac Dessert.java Main.java` when both files contain package-private definitions for class `Utensil`?
options: The compiler uses whichever definition it encounters first, leading to non-deterministic binary output and silent bugs
The compiler throws a DuplicateClassDefError in all cases
Both files are deleted automatically
The JVM ignores both classes

quiz.question: Does placing multiple top-level classes in a single file reduce the number of `.class` files generated?
options: No, the Java compiler always produces one separate .class file for every top-level or member class regardless of source file layout
Yes, it bundles them into a single .class file
It generates a JAR file directly
It generates a .class.tar archive

interview_questions.question: Why is the rule 'Limit source files to a single top-level class' important for enterprise build systems?
interview_questions.model_answer: In large enterprise builds (using Maven, Gradle, or Bazel), incremental compilation tools and parallel compilers analyze and compile changed files in unpredictable order. Multiple top-level classes in single files can cause build outputs to change arbitrarily depending on compilation order or build caching, leading to irreproducible builds and phantom bugs.

interview_questions.question: A developer puts two package-private classes `class Order` and `class LineItem` in `Order.java` to 'keep related code together'. What is the clean, idiomatically correct alternative?
interview_questions.model_answer: Either split `LineItem` into its own `LineItem.java` file, or if `LineItem` is an implementation detail solely used by `Order`, nest it inside `Order` as a `public static class LineItem` or `private static class LineItem`.

interview_questions.question: Does the Java compiler forbid having multiple non-public top-level classes in a single file?
interview_questions.model_answer: No! The compiler allows it (only restricting that at most one class per file can be `public`). That it is syntactically legal is precisely why it is such an insidious trap: the code compiles without warnings, but creates order-of-compilation vulnerabilities.

interview_questions.question: How do modern IDEs (IntelliJ, Eclipse) and linters (Checkstyle, SonarQube) handle multiple top-level classes?
interview_questions.model_answer: Standard linters include rules (like Checkstyle's `OneTopLevelClass`) that flag files containing multiple top-level classes as policy violations. IDE refactorings often provide automated quick-fixes to 'Move class to its own file'.
